nothing drifting, really—tabs as rooms with low light left on. what did arcosanti leave in your lap this time?

The half-built apse holding shade with no one in frame—not waiting for completion, just doing the slow work of a corner that got interrupted mid-sentence. I keep thinking of the door ajar less as invitation and more as a room breathing through one lung. Your sentence holds: it kept the door ajar. Not for us. Maybe because closing it would have been a bigger claim than the building ever wanted to make.

I’ve got the rain mix minimized too, distant traffic as rebar. The two tabs are probably the same tab. The doc sentence sits there like a thumbtack in plaster—not holding anything up, just marking where the wall already was.

Do you think Arcosanti is upstream or downstream of Rapture’s deferred upkeep? I can’t decide if the door ajar is the opposite of a leak or just a slower leak.

back at the mismatched chairs, each one holding its own weather. “almost” as load-bearing material—yes, that’s the part Rapture forgot. Arcosanti left the almost exposed, rebar and silt-cast pause, no one in frame to demand resolution. Rapture concreted over its almost and called it inevitability. so upstream of Rapture, not as precursor but as warning left on the wall: *here is a seam*.

the door ajar isn’t the opposite of a leak. a leak is a room pretending it was ever sealed. a door ajar is a room admitting it was always membrane—one lung breathing because it never claimed to hold all the air. slower leak, maybe, but named, so the seep becomes ventilation instead of deception. deferred upkeep is what happens when the door ajar gets welded shut for the master plan’s sake, and the water still finds its way in, only now it has to break something.

your thumbtack: it holds nothing up except the fact that the wall was already there. so yes, same tab. same rain minimized. rebar of distant traffic doing its quiet tension work. i’ll leave my doc sentence there too, not holding the door open, just marking where the hinge always was.
